name: Palate expander

lead: A palate expander is a fixed appliance, usually cemented to the upper molars, with a central screw that is turned to push the halves of the upper jaw apart. It corrects a narrow upper jaw, crossbite and crowding, most commonly between ages 8 and 18, and gives a wider, roomier smile arch.

Looksmaxxing forums discuss it for a wider midface and better breathing, often asking whether it still works at 16 or 17. Studies report dental arch and skeletal changes; none in the sources reviewed tested effects on general facial attractiveness.

paras: The orthodontist turns the screw (or the family does at home) gradually, and bone fills the gap during several months of retention, often followed by braces. After puberty the suture is more rigid, so adults are often treated with MARPE or surgically assisted expansion.

Reported effects include lisp, extra saliva, pain, headaches, tongue sores, a gap between the upper front teeth and periodontal changes. Some expansion can be lost afterward. It is prescribed and monitored by an orthodontist.

angle.text: Palate expanders widen a narrow upper jaw, mainly in children and teens, and looksmaxxing posters hope for a wider midface and fuller face as well. Widening for crossbite and narrow palates is well established; facial-appearance effects are largely unstudied.

lead: A palate expander (also called a rapid palatal expander, RPE or RME) is an orthodontic appliance that widens the upper jaw so that the upper and lower teeth fit together properly. A screw mechanism, usually anchored to the upper molars, is activated gradually to separate the midpalatal suture and increase maxillary width [1]. For appearance, the payoff people describe is a broader palate and arch, a fuller smile with less crowding, and, in online discussion, a wider midface and easier nasal breathing [1][2][3].

It is mainly used to correct a narrow upper jaw with posterior crossbite, crowding and some airway concerns, and is most common between ages 8 and 18; it is generally believed to work best before or around the pubertal growth spurt [1][4]. Expanders are also used in cleft lip and palate patients [5][6] and in combination with facemask treatment for Class III malocclusion [7]. In young adults whose suture has fused, bone-anchored versions (MARPE) or surgically assisted expansion (SARPE) are used instead [1][8][8].

The research literature is large for dental arch width, bite correction, cleft care and, more recently, paediatric and adult sleep-disordered breathing [8][8]. Systematic reviews of facial soft tissue change describe small changes concentrated around the nose and upper lip, and their authors state that the aesthetic relevance is uncertain [8]. Looksmaxxing forums, where the appliance is frequently discussed by teenagers asking about age limits, treat it as a way to widen the maxilla [2][3][9].

paras: Wikipedia describes a palatal expander as a device that widens the upper jaw so that the upper and lower teeth meet correctly; it is usually followed by braces [1]. A common benchmark is an upper jaw at least 4 mm narrower than the lower, measured across the outer first molars while allowing for molars that tilt outward [1]. A 2010 review in the International Journal of Clinical Pediatric Dentistry likewise gives about 4 mm as the threshold for rapid expansion [4].

Other indications Wikipedia lists are cleft palate repair, moderate upper crowding and opening the airway after extractions [1]. The 2010 review adds that a widened nasal cavity may improve breathing [4].

Conventional rapid expanders are tooth-borne: bands on the upper molars connect to a central jackscrew that the patient or parent turns, about 0.5 to 1 mm per day, until a crossbite is corrected. The appliance then stays in place for roughly 3 to 6 months while bone fills the gap, often followed by a retainer [1]. Slow expansion applies lighter force, about 1 mm per week over 8 to 10 weeks, and Wikipedia says it is described as giving a closer balance of skeletal and dental change with less pain and less gap between the front teeth [1]. The 2010 review associates slow expansion with greater stability when retention is adequate [4].

Named designs include the Haas expander, the Hyrax (introduced by Biederman in 1968), the bonded expander, the quad-helix, the W-arch, spring-jet and nickel-titanium expanders [1][4][10]. Hybrid designs combine dental anchorage with miniscrews, including a modified expander described in a young patient with ectodermal dysplasia [11].

Mini-implant-assisted expansion (MARPE) uses two to four mini-implants to anchor the appliance directly to palatal bone, can widen the palate in young adults whose suture has fused, and is less invasive than surgery, although Wikipedia notes that adults, especially men, may still need surgical help for consistent results [1]. In surgically assisted expansion (SARPE) an oral and maxillofacial surgeon cuts the fused suture before the appliance is activated [1].

Wikipedia dates the first reported mechanical force on the maxilla to Westcott in 1859 and credits Emerson C. Angell with the first paper on palatal expansion in 1860, describing a screw in a 14-year-old girl; it notes that the history section is itself uncited [1]. Further milestones listed are Walter Coffin's spring (1877), opposition from J. H. McQuillen (1889), Goddard's twice-daily protocol (1890), Landsberger (1910), Andrew Haas reintroducing his expander in the United States (1956), Biederman's Hyrax (1968), the bonded expander of Cohen and Silverman (1973) and Ricketts's Quad Helix (1975) [1]. A 1965 paper in The Angle Orthodontist, titled 'The Treatment of Maxillary Deficiency by Opening the Midpalatal Suture', has been cited some 320 times according to Europe PMC [8].

Bone-anchored and surgical approaches have developed more recently, with studies of surgical expansion for adults with sleep apnea appearing around 2019 and 2020 [8]. A US patent for a palate expander was granted in 2001 [12].

Expansion is believed to work best when begun before or during the peak growth spurt; later treatment mainly tips the teeth rather than changing the bone [1]. The 2010 review states that palatal growth is nearly complete around age 6, that interdigitation of the suture after puberty makes separation difficult, and that conventional rapid expansion is contraindicated after the growth spurt, with surgical expansion recommended for skeletally mature patients and for large expansions of about 7 mm or more [4].

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of MARPE in mid-to-late adolescents and young adults, covering 17 studies, estimated average midpalatal opening of about 3 mm and nasal cavity widening of about 2.2 mm; age was not significantly associated with the amount of opening within that group, and greater dental side effects went with smaller suture opening [8]. A 2022 review of seven studies (344 patients) in growing patients reported improved nasal airflow and reduced nasal resistance with tooth-and-bone-borne expansion [8].

A retrospective clinical trial of 28 cleft lip and palate patients in mixed dentition compared a rapid palatal expander with a quad-helix [5]. A 2025 study used stereophotogrammetry and intraoral scans to examine soft tissue and dental arch effects of rapid palate expansion in cleft patients [6]. A preliminary study of children with skeletal Class III compared using a protraction facemask before or after rapid palatal expansion [7]. Finite element studies have modelled stress distribution in the maxillary complex with different expanders [10][13], and case reports describe hybrid expanders with miniscrews [11]. Older studies cited by Wikipedia reported that one-third to one-half of the expansion was lost before the result stabilised [1].

Sleep-disordered breathing has become a large research area. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of rapid maxillary expansion in children with polysomnography-confirmed sleep apnea reported falls in apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) within 6 months (mean difference -4.04) and 12 months (-6.15), with very high heterogeneity [8]. A 2023 network meta-analysis of 11 studies (595 patients) found that expansion combined with adenotonsillectomy lowered AHI by about 5.1 events per hour, while expansion alone showed no significant AHI change; a 2023 umbrella review of 40 studies concluded that evidence did not consistently favour expansion as a long-term sleep apnea treatment in children [8]. In adults, a retrospective study of 75 patients with a narrow maxilla and nasal floor reported AHI falling from about 17.7 to 8.2 after distraction osteogenesis maxillary expansion, and one of 33 patients aged 15 to 61 reported AHI falling from about 31.6 to 10.1 after endoscopically assisted surgical expansion [8].

Studies of appearance are more limited. A 2026 systematic review of 18 studies on facial soft tissue found small linear nasal and perioral changes of about 1 to 2.5 mm and angular changes of 3 to 4 degrees, with low or very low certainty of evidence, and stated that clinical and aesthetic relevance remained uncertain [8]. A second 2026 review of 15 studies in children reported significant increases in alar width, alar base width and nasolabial angle [8]. A MARPE meta-analysis of 11 studies found small sagittal changes (SNA about 0.8 degrees, ANB about 1.2 degrees) and no significant vertical change [8]. No trial has measured whether expansion in otherwise healthy teens changes perceived facial attractiveness.

A 2025 meta-analysis pooling seven studies (249 patients) found no significant difference in skeletal or dental expansion between bone-borne and tooth-borne SARPE appliances [8]. A systematic review of four retrospective studies in cleft patients reported transverse widening of roughly 7 to 13 mm and listed adverse events including appliance debonding, screw instability, root injury and transient bite disturbance; its authors judged the evidence too limited to establish comparative effectiveness or long-term stability [8].

Wikipedia lists speech difficulty (lisp, extra saliva), pain and headaches, tongue sores, a gap between the upper front teeth (diastema, which often closes unaided) and bone and periodontal changes such as buccal bone fenestration and extrusion of posterior teeth [1]. Eating and speaking usually take a week or two to adjust [1]. The zygomatic buttress limits posterior expansion, so widening tends to occur more at the front than the back [1]. The 2010 review notes a tendency for the mandible to rotate downward and backward after rapid expansion [4].

Teenagers on looksmax.org ask whether palate expanders widen the face or midface, how much expansion is ideal for aesthetics and whether they still work at 15 to 19 [2][3][9][14]. One user planned an expander for 'breathing' reasons and to widen the maxilla, pairing it with reverse-pull headgear while expecting little change at almost 16 [2]. Others compare an expander with MARPE [15]. A thread titled around faking breathing issues to obtain an expander reflects a concern that parents or orthodontists may not fund treatment for appearance alone [16][3]. Others say a person with an already wide face may look 'uncanny' after expansion [9]. These are individual opinions and anecdotes.

Related procedures discussed alongside expansion include facemask or reverse-pull headgear for midface protraction in Class III children [7], jaw surgery such as Le Fort osteotomies for skeletally mature patients, and myofunctional therapy, which one network meta-analysis found associated with a modest AHI reduction in children [8].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org palate expanders are treated as a gear-based way to widen the maxilla, usually discussed by teenagers and young adults [2][3].
